chunks.title: Neonatal & infant eye examination
chunks.tldr: Every newborn: symmetric anatomy + red reflex each eye. Fixation on a face; smooth pursuit may be jerky for 2 months. Pupils react from ~29 wk gestation, reliable from 32 wk; anisocoria 0.5 mm in 20% — but ptosis + anisocoria → Horner → neuroblastoma. Dilate: phenylephrine 2.5% + cyclopentolate 1%/tropicamide 1%; premature/light irides → Cyclomydril (cyclopentolate 0.2% + phenylephrine 1%). Newborn disc grey (pink by 2 y), no physiological cup; retinal haemorrhages in up to 50% of births, clear in weeks. Infant fundus grey, no foveal reflex until 3–4 months. Schedule: neonate (red reflex) → 6 mo (fixation, alignment) → 4 y (acuity) → 5–16 y every 2 y; colour 8–12 y.

chunks.title: Vision & refraction in children
chunks.tldr: Approx VA: 2 mo 6/120, 6 mo 6/30, 1 y 6/15, 3 y 6/6. Pre-verbal: fix & follow, objection to occlusion (covering the good eye upsets the child), preferential looking (overestimates amblyopic VA), OKN, VEP. From ~4 y: tumbling E, Lea, HOTV; stereo (Random Dot E, Titmus) from 3–4 y. Cycloplegic refraction: cyclopentolate 1% ×2, 5 min apart, 30 min before; atropine 1% ointment daily ×2–3 days for esotropia/dark irides — warn of toxicity (fever, flushing, tachycardia). Ages 2–6: 80% hyperopic, 5% myopic; only ~10% need specs before 7–8 y; myopia appears 6–9 y and grows through puberty; anisometropia → amblyopia.

cards.q: Signs of atropine toxicity in a child?
cards.a: Fever, flushed dry skin, tachycardia, irritability/confusion.

chunks.title: Congenital anomalies of globe, lids, cornea, iris
chunks.tldr: Anophthalmos (no optic vesicle), cystic eye (no invagination), coloboma (fissure fails to close — inferonasal), cryptophthalmos (lids unseparated). Nanophthalmos (small but normal) vs microphthalmos (abnormal). Ptosis (levator dystrophy, Horner, III) → amblyopia. Lid coloboma (Goldenhar) → repair. Cloudy cornea DDx (STUMPED): Sclerocornea, Tears in Descemet (glaucoma, forceps), Ulcer, Metabolic (MPS — Hurler), Peters, Endothelial dystrophy (CHED), Dermoid. Megalocornea: X-linked, clear. Aniridia (PAX6, AD): glaucoma, foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus; sporadic (WAGR, 11p13) → Wilms tumour — renal US every 3 months to age 8. Axenfeld-Rieger, Peters (neural crest/PAX6) → glaucoma. Heterochromia: congenital Horner, inflammation.

cards.a: Wilms tumour (WAGR syndrome, 11p13 deletion including WT1).

cards.q: Causes of a cloudy cornea at birth?
cards.a: Congenital glaucoma, forceps injury (Descemet breaks), Peters anomaly, CHED, sclerocornea, mucopolysaccharidosis, dermoid, infection.

chunks.title: Congenital cataract, glaucoma, PHPV, optic nerve, NLDO
chunks.tldr: Cataract: AD commonest in developed world; rubella in developing; position dates onset. Visually significant → surgery within ~2 months, then CL/IOL + amblyopia therapy; bilateral: short interval. Congenital glaucoma: photophobia, haze, big cornea; DDx forceps, anterior segment dysgenesis, MPS (no enlargement). Hyaloid remnants: Mittendorf dot (lens), Bergmeister papilla (disc); PHPV/PFV → leukocoria, microphthalmia. Choroidal coloboma (CHARGE, Aicardi, Goldenhar). ONH (double-ring): septo-optic dysplasia → hypoglycaemia, jaundice, growth failure, DI → endocrine + MRI. Congenital NLDO: 30% early epiphora, 6% persist; massage + antibiotics; probing ~1 y (earlier if dacryocystitis); intubation/balloon/DCR. Crouzon: craniosynostosis, shallow orbits/proptosis, hypertelorism, strabismus, optic atrophy.
chunks.hook: Watery eye in a baby: blocked duct (common) vs glaucoma (photophobia, big cornea).

chunks.title: The visually inattentive baby
chunks.tldr: After excluding ONH, albinism, high refractive error: LCA and cone dystrophy (roving nystagmus, oculodigital sign eye-poking; ERG confirms), cortical/cerebral visual impairment (prematurity, HIE; commonest cause in developed countries; normal eyes, MRI), ocular motor apraxia (can't start horizontal saccades — head thrusts; vision fine), delayed visual maturation (sees after 2–6 months; normal if isolated).
chunks.hook: Baby poking its eyes = retinal dystrophy (LCA) — get an ERG.

chunks.title: Ophthalmia neonatorum & childhood uveitis
chunks.tldr: Chlamydia = commonest infectious cause in US; day 5–14; inclusions, IF/PCR; oral erythromycin (also treats nasopharynx → prevents pneumonitis). Bacterial day 2–5 (staph, Haemophilus, strep, gonococcus, Pseudomonas — corneal risk); gonococcus → IV/IM ceftriaxone (cefotaxime if jaundiced). HSV: giant cells; keratitis <6 months → admit, LP-PCR, systemic acyclovir. Test/treat baby for other STIs; treat mother and partners. Childhood uveitis: HLA-B27, intermediate, Fuchs, idiopathic; JIA (oligoarticular, ANA+ girls) silent → screening; watch steroid effects on growth.

cards.q: Why give systemic rather than topical treatment for chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis?
cards.a: To eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent chlamydial pneumonitis.

chunks.title: Retinopathy of prematurity
chunks.tldr: Risks: low gestational age & birth weight, oxygen, acidosis, apnoea, PDA, sepsis, transfusions, IVH. Vessels reach nasal ora at 8 mo, temporal at 9 mo. Stages: 1 demarcation line, 2 ridge, 3 extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, 4 subtotal RD, 5 total RD; zone I (around disc) worst; plus disease = posterior venous dilation + arterial tortuosity. Screen: BW ≤1500 g or GA ≤30 wk (or sicker 1500–2000 g); start at 31 wk PMA if GA ≤27 wk, else 4 wk chronological age; until vascularised/regressed. Treat (Type 1): zone I any stage + plus, zone I stage 3, zone II stage 2–3 + plus → laser (diode indirect) or intravitreal anti-VEGF (BEAT-ROP: zone I); vitrectomy for 4–5 (poor). Late: myopia, strabismus, cataract, angle closure, dragged disc/macula, retinal breaks.
points: Screening/treatment can cause apnoea/cardiorespiratory arrest — neonatal team present.

cards.a: Dilation and tortuosity of posterior pole retinal vessels indicating active, severe ROP.
Birth weight ≤1500 g or gestational age ≤30 weeks, plus selected larger/older unstable infants.

chunks.title: Leukocoria, strabismus, amblyopia, abuse & dyslexia
chunks.tldr: Leukocoria (or absent red-eye in photos): retinoblastoma (90% by 3 y), cataract, ROP, PHPV, Coats, toxocara, high refractive error → urgent referral. Strabismus (~2–4%) after 3 months always refer; never 'grow out of it'. Amblyopia: critical period to ~8 y; strabismus, anisometropia, bilateral high hyperopia/astigmatism; specs → patch/atropine; screen by 4 y. Shaken baby (abusive head trauma): multilayered retinal haemorrhages (intra-, pre-retinal, vitreous) to the periphery ± retinoschisis, with subdural haemorrhage, often no external injury; in <3 y strongly suggestive once blood disorders excluded; document carefully, involve paediatrics. Dyslexia: central language-processing problem, not visual; treat any refractive error/strabismus; 'vision therapy'/coloured lenses unproven.
chunks.hook: Haemorrhages everywhere in a baby without a bump = abuse until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Retinal findings typical of abusive head trauma?
cards.a: Numerous multilayered haemorrhages extending to the ora, often with perimacular retinoschisis/folds.

cards.q: Is dyslexia caused by eye problems?
cards.a: No — it's a central language-processing disorder; vision therapy has no proven benefit.
